name: fennick
author: school-home
description:
fennick v3 (direction: school and home life) - A BOOKSHELF WITH BOOKS TIPPING OVER. PRIVATE; never shown to players.

WHY v3 (demo-economy pass, 2026-09-04). v2 measured 0 %/100 % over two Opus players in the OLD 6-round / 6-demo format: the crack needed a THIRD demo and ~40 candidate height rules, because the answer's heights were free and had to be searched to match a four-letter tally. In the new format (7 classes, 4 rounds, ~60 probes per class per round, 3 demos per team for the whole game) that budget does not exist. v3 removes the search entirely: the HEIGHTS ARE NOW IN THE CLUE. The clue is the finished shelf with every book standing upright, and the answer is that same picture with the right books tipped over. Nothing else changed about the rule.

CLUE = the upright picture + the shelf + one line "<n> fall".
  ...pictures rows (right-stripped), the tallest book's cap on the top row...
  bottom picture row = the LAYOUT: an uppercase letter = a book in that slot, "." = an empty slot
  a row of "=" as wide as the shelf
  a line "5 fall" - how many books fall over (the count only; v2's four-letter tally is gone)
The first two and last two slots are always books, so "is the outside of the shelf a wall or a hole?"
never has to be guessed and the scorer can index two slots either way without a bounds test (load-bearing:
do not relax the anchoring). Width 34-42 slots, 2-7 picture rows, clue 181-342 chars.
A book of height h standing upright is a solid bar of h copies of its letter in its own column with a
"_" cap one row above it. Heights are uniform random 1..hmax (hmax in 4,5,6) - deliberately arbitrary,
and now GIVEN, so there is no height formula to hunt (that red herring ate v2's losing player's whole game).

ANSWER = the clue with the falling books drawn tipped. A leaning book keeps its foot letter in its own slot
on the bottom row; its other h-1 letters and its cap move one column across into the empty slot it falls
into, and its cap becomes "/" when it leans right, "\" when it leans left. Everything else - the standing
books, the shelf row, the "<n> fall" line - is copied unchanged. The answer is therefore UNIQUE per clue.
The trailing "<n> fall" line may be included or omitted; both score 1.

RULE (unchanged since v1, one clause): a book falls over iff exactly one of its two neighbouring slots is
empty (a book with books on both sides is held up; a book with gaps on both sides has nothing pushing it
over), the slot two along in that direction holds a book (a two-slot gap is out of reach), and that book is
STRICTLY taller (equal heights and both stay up). Said in one breath: "a book falls over if there is a gap
on one side and a taller book just across it."

EVERY DEMO TEACHES THE WHOLE RULE. generate() plants, in every instance: >= 4 tipped books (mean 4.3,
range 4-9); at least one pair of EQUAL-height books facing each other across a one-slot gap, both standing
(100 % of clues - so ">=" instead of ">" is visibly wrong in every demo); at least one book with gaps on
both sides, at least two high, standing (98.5 %); at least two books beside a two-slot gap, standing
(100 %); and ~4.6 books that stand beside a gap because the book across it is SHORTER (100 %). So a single
demo shows the positive case and all three near-miss cases side by side. The demo is a picture pair (clue,
solution) that differs only in the tipped books.

THE FOOTHOLD (lever 7). 12.7 % of clues (measured over 8000 seeds) say "0 fall": nothing tips, and the
correct answer IS the clue's picture returned unchanged. A demo-less player who echoes the clue therefore
scores ~13 %, which is the intended floor, and a player who notices the count line scores exactly that 13 %
deliberately. The cost is that ~13 % of demo requests land on a shelf where nothing falls (it still teaches
the drawing convention and the copy-the-count-line rule, but not the tipping rule); 0.075 was chosen for
the zero-tip branch as the balance between that dud-demo risk and a foothold comfortably above 10 %.

WITNESS TABLE (2000 fresh clues, shipped scorer; templates render with the TRUE drawing convention, i.e.
they model a player who has seen a demo and holds the wrong rule):
  clue picture returned unchanged           13.0 %   <- the foothold
  all books upright, tally line dropped     13.0 %   <- same thing, the lenient form
  every book tipped into a gap               0.0 %
  tip toward any taller neighbour (no gap)   0.0 %
  tip toward its one gap, height ignored     0.0 %
  tip toward any gap, height ignored         0.0 %
  near-miss ">=" instead of ">"              0.0 %   (killed by the planted equal-height pair)
  near-miss "gaps on both sides count too"  19.2 %
  near-miss "nearest book beyond any gap"   14.2 %
  random tilts                               0.0 %
  demo replay (another clue's answer)        0.0 %
  constant string                            0.0 %
  junk / empty / clue fragments              0.0 %
  TRUE RULE (solve)                        100.0 %
No template exceeds 20 %. The two surviving near-misses are deliberate: they are the gradient a player
climbs (a wrong-but-close rule scores like the foothold, the exact rule scores 100 %), and both are
visibly contradicted by every demo.

WELL-FORMEDNESS (28 hand-built attacks, all 0): no shelf row, two shelf rows, shelf of dashes, shelf one
short, leading blank row, rows reversed, mirrored picture, caps removed, tilt marks straightened (= the
clue, on a clue with n > 0), tilt marks swapped / <-> \, dots instead of spaces, wrong count line, count
line forced to 0, answer plus a junk line, 4000 chars of junk, the empty string. Declared leniencies:
trailing newlines/whitespace, rows right-padded or right-stripped, junk beyond column W of a row, and the
final count line present or absent. Nothing about the rule can be smuggled in through them.

ENGINEERING (8000 fresh seeds; 1000 solved and scored). generate avg 0.12 ms, p99 0.52 ms, max 1.1 ms,
0 fallback uses; solve avg 0.03 ms max 0.06 ms (v2's height search is gone); score avg 0.030 ms max 0.093 ms
and <= 0.09 ms on junk; scorer 496/512 chars, solve 1045 chars; clue 181-342 chars, solution 184-342 chars;
3000/3000 clues distinct and deterministic; 1000/1000 solve() outputs score 1.

INTENDED SPLIT. With a demo: the diff between the two pictures is the whole rule, so a player who reads it
as a picture ("these four books fell into the gap next to them, and the book across the gap is taller")
cracks it inside two rounds; a player who reads it as bookkeeping lands on one of the two 14-19 % near-misses
instead. Without a demo: the clue is already a drawn shelf and a count, so a well-formed attempt is obvious
(send the picture back, maybe with something tipped) and the "0 fall" instances pay ~13 %.
solve:
def solve(clue):
    P = clue.split("\n")
    T = P.pop()                                   # the "<n> fall" line, copied through
    B = P.pop()                                   # the shelf
    W = len(B)
    P = [x.ljust(W) for x in P]
    L = P[-1]                                     # bottom row of the picture = the layout
    M = len(P)
    H = [M - 1 - len(z) + len(z.lstrip()) for z in map("".join, zip(*P))]
    g = lambda j: 0 <= j < W and L[j] == "."
    Q = [[" "] * W for _ in range(M)]
    Q[M - 1] = list(L)
    for i in range(W):
        h = H[i]
        if not h:
            continue
        d = g(i + 1) - g(i - 1)                   # +1 gap on the right only, -1 on the left only
        b = 1 if d and 0 <= i + 2 * d < W and H[i + 2 * d] > h else 0
        j = i + b * d                             # a falling book's body moves into the gap
        for t in range(1, h):
            Q[M - 1 - t][j] = L[i]
        Q[M - 1 - h][j] = "_/\\"[b * d]
    return "\n".join("".join(x).rstrip() for x in Q) + "\n" + B + "\n" + T
